Rain has its own language. Some days it taps lightly at the window like someone trying not to wake the house. Other days it arrives all at once, drumming with authority, turning sidewalks into mirrors and turning the air into something clean enough to drink. When the rain is steady, the city seems to slow down—not because it truly does, but because you start paying attention to smaller things: the way water beads on leaves, the hush that forms between sounds, the soft blur of headlights gliding through wet streets.

I used to think weather was something happening to the world, like a background painting. But lately I feel it happening inside me, too. A storm makes my thoughts run faster, as if they want to outrun the lightning. A drizzle makes me patient. I find myself lingering over ordinary routines: stirring tea slowly, folding a shirt carefully, watching clouds gather without needing to understand them.

There’s comfort in that. Rain doesn’t ask for permission. It doesn’t negotiate. It just arrives, does its work, and then—sometimes suddenly—lets the light return. Afterward, everything looks briefly new, as if the world has been edited: edges sharpened, colors brightened, the air clarified.

Maybe that’s why I like it. Rain reminds me that change can be both rough and renewing. It can wash away what’s tired, without demanding I be anything other than present.
